pointers.sentence: A server is pointed at the project's WSGI or ASGI module, `wsgi.py` or `asgi.py`, which startproject also writes; importing it calls `get_wsgi_application` or `get_asgi_application`, which calls `django.setup` and then makes the handler (`django/core/wsgi.py:get_wsgi_application`, `django/core/asgi.py:get_asgi_application`).

A server is pointed at the project's WSGI or ASGI module, `wsgi.py` or `asgi.py`, which startproject also writes; importing it calls `get_wsgi_application` or `get_asgi_application`, which calls `django.setup` and then makes the handler (`django/core/wsgi.py:get_wsgi_application`, `django/core/asgi.py:get_asgi_application`).

**The settings**, `settings`, a `LazySettings`, exist as soon as `django.conf` is imported, but read the settings module only the first time they are needed, which in `setup` is at once, and then keep its values (`django/conf/__init__.py:LazySettings._setup`).

**The app registry**, `apps`, an `Apps`, imports every installed application and then its models, and holds an `AppConfig` for each application and every model class but the abstract ones (`django/__init__.py:setup`, `django/apps/registry.py:Apps.populate`).

**The app registry**, `apps`, an `Apps`, imports every installed application and then its models, and holds an `AppConfig` for each application and every model class but the abstract ones (`django/__init__.py:setup`, `django/apps/registry.py:Apps.populate`).
When it is made it turns the `MIDDLEWARE` setting into the **middleware chain**, the middleware nested one inside the next, and keeps it (`django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler.load_middleware`).

When the request reaches the centre of the chain, the handler itself asks **the resolver**, a `URLResolver` made from the root URLconf on first use and kept, to match the request's path against the URL patterns, and it returns the view and the arguments the path supplied (`django/urls/resolvers.py:URLResolver.resolve`).
**The view** is any callable that takes a request and returns a response; Django asks of it only that it return one (`django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler.check_response`).

**The model**, a subclass of `Model`, is the class through which the application reads and writes the rows of a table, a field in most cases standing for a column; its options, kept as `Model._meta` (an `Options`), hold what Django knows about it: its fields, its table, its relations, its ordering (`django/db/models/base.py:ModelBase.__new__`).
The admin, the model forms and the migrations derive what they need from `_meta` (`django/forms/models.py:fields_for_model`, `django/db/migrations/state.py:ModelState.from_model`).
The admin, the model forms and the migrations derive what they need from `_meta` (`django/forms/models.py:fields_for_model`, `django/db/migrations/state.py:ModelState.from_model`).

**The queryset**, a `QuerySet`, is a lazy description of a query, built up by chained calls, which a `SQLCompiler` of the database's backend turns into SQL when its results are first needed (`django/db/models/query.py:QuerySet._fetch_all`).

**The template engine**, an `Engine`, finds a template by name through its loaders and compiles it into a tree of nodes, which is rendered with a context (`django/template/engine.py:Engine.get_template`).

The `TEMPLATES` setting names not the engine but a **template backend**, `DjangoTemplates`, which wraps it in the interface every backend shares, so that Jinja2 can stand in its place (`django/template/backends/django.py:DjangoTemplates`, `deps:final/0182-multiple-template-engines.rst`).

The `TEMPLATES` setting names not the engine but a **template backend**, `DjangoTemplates`, which wraps it in the interface every backend shares, so that Jinja2 can stand in its place (`django/template/backends/django.py:DjangoTemplates`, `deps:final/0182-multiple-template-engines.rst`).

Another way into a process is a management command: `manage.py` calls `execute_from_command_line`, which calls `django.setup` and then runs the command (`django/core/management/__init__.py:ManagementUtility.execute`).

The view returns a response, which goes back out through the middleware in the reverse order and on to the server, and when the response has been sent it is closed, which sends `request_finished`, one of the **signals** by which a part of Django tells any receiver that something has happened (`django/http/response.py:HttpResponseBase.close`).

Django requires two libraries beside Python, asgiref for the bridge between synchronous and asynchronous code and sqlparse for splitting and parsing SQL, and on Windows a third, tzdata (`django:pyproject.toml`); it imports others where a feature needs them, from Pillow for images to Jinja2 for a second template engine.
